title: Choices that multiply
objectives: Count the outcomes of several choices in a row with the product rule.
Tell when choices multiply and when they add.

screens.title: Choices that multiply
screens.prose: You get dressed, order lunch or set a password by making one choice after another. We will count the possible results without writing every one out.
You have 3 shirts and 2 pairs of trousers. The tree shows each shirt, then each pair of trousers that could go with it.

state.caption: Each path from the left to the right is one outfit

screens.question: How many different outfits can you wear?

hints.text: Each outfit is one path from the root to a leaf on the right.
Follow the white shirt: it ends in two leaves.
Each of the 3 shirts ends in 2 leaves. Count all the leaves.

feedback.correct: Three shirts, each with two pairs of trousers: 6 outfits.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the leaves on the right of the tree.

byKey.added: You added the 3 shirts and the 2 trousers. But every shirt goes with both pairs, so each shirt gives 2 outfits.
byKey.shirts: You counted the shirts only. Each shirt splits again into 2 outfits.

explain.text: You counted the leaves: each of the 3 shirts splits into 2. That is 3 groups of 2, so $3 \times 2 = 6$ outfits.

screens.prose: Now add a third choice: trainers or boots. Every outfit from before splits once more. Tap a leaf to select that outfit, and tap again to clear it.
screens.question: Tap every outfit that uses the blue shirt.

hints.text: Start at the Blue branch and follow every path to the right.
Everything to the right of Blue uses the blue shirt.

feedback.correct: Four outfits use the blue shirt: 2 trousers, each with 2 pairs of shoes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap the leaves at the far right that start from Blue.

byKey.shirt-only: You tapped the blue shirt branch itself. An outfit is a whole path, so tap the shoe branches at the far right.
byKey.one-trouser: You found the outfits with jeans. The blue shirt also goes with chinos, so two more count.
byKey.b-j: You tapped a trouser branch. Each outfit ends at a shoe branch on the far right.
byKey.b-c: You tapped a trouser branch. Each outfit ends at a shoe branch on the far right.

explain.text: The blue shirt leads to 4 outfits: 2 trousers, each with 2 shoes. The white and grey shirts lead to 4 each as well. So there are 3 groups of 4, which is $3 \times 2 \times 2 = 12$.

screens.prose: Each new stage multiplied the count: 3 shirts, then $\times 2$ for trousers, then $\times 2$ for shoes. Counting this way is the **product rule**: multiply the number of choices at each stage.
screens.question: You add a jacket, one of 3. Every outfit can take any jacket. How many outfits now?

hints.text: What happens to each of the 12 leaves when a jacket stage is added?
Every leaf splits into 3 new leaves.
12 outfits, each with 3 jackets: multiply.

feedback.correct: Each of the 12 outfits splits 3 ways: 36.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each outfit so far can take any of the 3 jackets.

byKey.added: You added 3 jackets to the 12 outfits. Each outfit takes any jacket, so each one becomes 3 outfits.
byKey.forgot: You kept the count at 12. The jacket is a new stage, so every leaf splits again.
byKey.no-shoes: You multiplied 3, 2 and 3 and left out the shoes. All four stages count.

explain.text: The jacket stage splits each of the 12 leaves into 3. So the count is $3 \times 2 \times 2 \times 3 = 36$. Adding a stage multiplies; it never just adds.

screens.prose: A café meal deal is a main, a side and a drink. There are 4 mains, 3 sides and 2 drinks. Only the Pie branch is drawn out; the other mains are folded.
screens.question: How many different meal deals are there?

hints.text: How many meals start with Pie?
The Pie branch ends in 6 leaves.
Each of the 4 mains has the same 6 endings. Multiply.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the meals under Pie, then use the same count for every main.

byKey.added: You added 4, 3 and 2. Each main goes with every side and every drink, so the stages multiply.
byKey.one-main: You counted the meals under Pie only. Pasta, Curry and Risotto have 6 each as well.

explain.text: Pie leads to $3 \times 2 = 6$ meals, and so does each folded main. So there are $4 \times 3 \times 2 = 24$ meal deals.

screens.prose: Late in the day the juice runs out. Water is the only drink left, but a meal deal still needs a drink.
screens.question: How many meal deals are there now?

hints.text: How many leaves come off each side now?
Each side has one drink branch.
The drink stage has 1 choice. Multiply $4 \times 3 \times 1$.

feedback.correct: A stage with one choice multiplies by 1: $4 \times 3 \times 1 = 12$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The drink stage still exists, but it has only one choice.

byKey.unchanged: You kept both drinks. Only water is left, so each main and side gives one meal, not two.
byKey.added: You added 4, 3 and 1. The stages still multiply.
byKey.dropped: You treated one choice as no choice. Water still completes every meal, so nothing is lost but the juice.

explain.text: The drink stage has 1 choice, and multiplying by 1 changes nothing: $4 \times 3 \times 1 = 12$. If no drink at all were left, the stage would have 0 choices. Then $4 \times 3 \times 0 = 0$ meals could be completed.

screens.prose: A code is a row of characters, each 0 or 1. The tree draws every code with 3 characters.
screens.question: How many codes have 5 characters?

hints.text: How many codes have 3 characters? What does one more character do to that count?
Each extra character splits every leaf in two.
3 characters give 8. Two more characters double it twice.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each character is a stage with 2 choices.

byKey.times: You multiplied 5 by 2. Each character multiplies the count by 2, so it is 2 five times over.
byKey.squared: You worked out $5^2$. It is 2 multiplied by itself 5 times, $2^5$.
byKey.added: You added 2 and 5. Each character multiplies the count by 2, so it is $2^5 = 32$.
byKey.three: That is the count for 3 characters, the tree on screen. Two more characters double it twice.

explain.text: Every character is a stage with 2 choices, so 5 characters give $2^5 = 32$ codes. The tree for 3 characters has $2^3 = 8$ leaves. Each extra character doubles the count.

screens.prose: A menu lists 3 starters and 4 mains, 7 dishes in all. A two-course meal is one starter followed by one main. The mains are folded away in the tree.
screens.question: How many different two-course meals are there?

options.why: You added the 3 starters and the 4 mains. That counts single dishes. Each starter goes with every main, so the stages multiply.
You counted the mains only. Each of the 3 starters leads to all 4 mains.
You counted soup then fish and fish then soup. The starter always comes first, so each meal is counted once.

hints.text: Pick soup as your starter. How many meals can follow it?
Soup can be followed by any of the 4 mains.
Each of the 3 starters gives 4 meals.

feedback.correct: Each of 3 starters goes with each of 4 mains: 12.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the meals that start with soup first.

byKey.added: You added the dishes on the menu. A meal is a starter and a main, so each starter gives 4 meals.

explain.text: A meal is a starter **and then** a main: two stages, so $3 \times 4 = 12$. Adding, $3 + 4 = 7$, answers a different question. It counts the ways to order **one** dish, a starter or a main.

screens.prose: Each time, you multiplied the choices at every stage. If stage 1 has $n_1$ choices, stage 2 has $n_2$, and so on up to stage $k$: $$\text{outcomes} = n_1 \times n_2 \times \cdots \times n_k$$ This needs each stage to offer the same number of choices, whatever came before.
screens.question: Which of these counts is found by adding, not multiplying?

options.text: One dish: either a starter or a main
A starter and then a main
options.why: That is two stages, one after the other. Each starter goes with every main, so it multiplies.
That is four stages, one digit each. Each digit goes with every choice of the others, so it multiplies.

hints.text: Which choice is a single pick, not one pick after another?
The product rule needs stages in a row. A single pick from two lists is one stage.

feedback.correct: A single pick from two separate lists adds.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the one that is a single pick.

explain.text: A starter **or** a main is one choice from 7 dishes: $3 + 4$. A starter **and then** a main is two stages: $3 \times 4$. Multiply across stages; add across separate options for one stage.

screens.prose: A code has $n$ characters, and each character is a digit from 0 to 9. Complete the count: $$\underbrace{10 \times 10 \times \cdots \times 10}_{n \text{ stages}} = \; ?$$
screens.question: Write the number of codes in terms of $n$.

hints.text: For 1 character there are 10 codes. For 2 there are $10 \times 10$.
Each stage multiplies by the same 10.
Multiplying 10 by itself $n$ times is a power of 10.

feedback.correct: Ten choices at each of $n$ stages: $10^n$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each of the $n$ stages multiplies the count by 10.

byKey.times: You wrote $10n$, which adds 10 for each stage. Each stage multiplies by 10.
byKey.power: You swapped the base and the power. The 10 is repeated $n$ times, so it is $10^n$.

explain.text: Each of the $n$ characters is a stage with 10 choices. The product rule multiplies 10 by itself $n$ times, giving $10^n$. So 4 characters give $10^4 = 10\,000$ codes.

screens.prose: A backtest sweeps a trading rule's settings: 4 lookback windows, 3 entry signals and 2 position sizes. It runs every combination once. Each run costs £0.40 of cloud time. Only the 10-day branch is drawn out.
screens.question: What does the full sweep cost?

hints.text: First count the runs. How many sit under the 10-day branch?
The 10-day branch ends in $3 \times 2 = 6$ runs.
$4 \times 3 \times 2 = 24$ runs, each at £0.40.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the runs with the product rule, then price them.

byKey.added: You added 4, 3 and 2 to get 9 runs. Every lookback is tried with every signal and size, so they multiply.
byKey.drawn: You priced the 6 runs drawn out. The other three lookbacks have 6 runs each too.
byKey.runs: You found the number of runs, 24. Each one costs £0.40, so multiply by that too.

explain.text: The sweep has $4 \times 3 \times 2 = 24$ runs, so it costs $24 \times \text{£}0.40 = \text{£}9.60$. A fourth setting with 5 values would multiply the bill by 5, to £48.00. Sweeps grow fast, which is why quants prune them.

ideas: Choices made one after another multiply: each stage splits every path so far.
A stage with one choice multiplies by 1, and a stage with none makes the count 0.
One pick from separate lists adds; a pick from each list in turn multiplies.

formula.name: The product rule
formula.note: Stage $i$ has $n_i$ choices, whatever was picked before.

summary.trap: Adding the choices at each stage counts single items, not combinations. Stages in a row multiply.

quiz.prose: A PIN is 4 digits, each from 0 to 9. Digits may repeat, so 0070 is allowed.
quiz.question: How many PINs are there?

options.why: You multiplied 10 by the 4 places. Each place multiplies the count by 10, so it is $10^4$.
You took the largest PIN. 0000 is a PIN too, so there is one more.
You stopped digits repeating. This PIN may use a digit more than once.

feedback.correct: Ten choices at each of 4 places: $10^4$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Treat each digit as a stage with 10 choices.

explain.text: Each of the 4 digits has 10 choices, so there are $10 \times 10 \times 10 \times 10 = 10\,000$ PINs. They run from 0000 to 9999.

quiz.prose: A trader will open one position today. It is either one of 5 shares or one of 3 bond funds.
quiz.question: How many choices does she have?

options.why: You multiplied, as if she picked a share and a fund. She picks one or the other, so the lists add.
You counted the shares only. The 3 bond funds are choices too.
You counted the two kinds of asset. Within each kind she still picks one item.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Is this one pick or two picks in a row?

explain.text: She makes one pick from two separate lists, so the counts add: $5 + 3 = 8$. A share **and** a fund would be two stages: $5 \times 3 = 15$.

quiz.prose: A sandwich bar offers 3 breads and 5 fillings. You can also choose to add cheese or not.
quiz.question: How many different sandwiches are there?

options.why: You did not count the cheese stage. With or without cheese is a choice of 2, so it doubles.
You added 3, 5 and 2. Each bread goes with every filling and both cheese options.
You added one sandwich for the cheese. Every one of the 15 can take cheese, so each becomes two.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The cheese question is a stage with 2 choices.

explain.text: There are three stages: bread, filling, cheese or not. That gives $3 \times 5 \times 2 = 30$. Saying no is still one of the choices at a stage.

quiz.prose: A ticker code is 2 letters from A to Z followed by 1 digit from 0 to 9. Letters may repeat, as in AA7.
quiz.question: How many ticker codes are there?

options.why: You added 26, 26 and 10. The three places are stages, so they multiply.
You stopped the second letter repeating the first. Here letters may repeat.
You counted the two letters but left out the digit. The digit stage multiplies by 10.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the choices at each of the three places, then multiply.

explain.text: The first letter has 26 choices, the second 26 and the digit 10. So there are $26 \times 26 \times 10 = 6760$ codes.
